executive_summary: The dominant thread running through today's content is the fragility and active dismantling of trusted institutions — whether journalistic, geopolitical, or developmental. The most acute example comes from breaking news, where veteran CBS anchor Scott Pelley's accusation that CBS News leadership is 'murdering' 60 Minutes signals not merely internal corporate drama but the collapse of a flagship institution of American accountability journalism. This connects directly to the Foreign Affairs newsletter, which examines the end of foreign aid and how migration patterns empower authoritarian regimes — both stories about the unraveling of post-war liberal infrastructure that once provided stability and democratic norms. The Economist's war analysis adds another layer, drawing lessons from eight years of conflict to suggest that institutional assumptions about security and alliances are being stress-tested to their limits. Taken together, today's content makes a coherent and urgent argument: the institutional architecture that democratic societies built over the last 80 years — in media, foreign policy, and international security — is under simultaneous pressure from within and without, and the consequences of that erosion are no longer theoretical.

AI isn't killing jobs (yet)
items.blurb: Despite the warning by some of an imminent jobs apocalypse that will destroy much, if not most, of such work, or the rumblings about a "permanent underclass," there's scant evidence that AI has yet had any large-scale impact on the US labor market. After digging into the data, David Rotman has three charts to show why.

items.headline: Build, buy, or borrow? Agentic AI decisions you can stand behind
items.blurb: Agentic AI is moving from experimentation to operational reality—fast. Yet many organizations are stuck at the same decision point: build in-house, buy off-the-shelf, or partner? Success depends on redesigning how work gets done—using a federated mix of agents anchored by a unified control system for trust and governance.

newsletters.title: The War Room: Eight years of conflict—what I learned

items.headline: Eight years of conflict—what I learned
items.blurb: A valedictory effort to reconcile the myriad lessons from eight years as defence editor, a period that has seen two system-shaping wars, one in Ukraine and the other a series of connected campaigns across the Middle East, among other conflicts.

items.headline: The increasing transparency of the modern battlefield
items.blurb: Near the front line in Ukraine, it seems virtually impossible to move without being seen or struck, typically by a drone. This transparency is always partial and depends on geography—consider how Iran has successfully hidden so many of its missile launchers despite American and Israeli air dominance.

items.headline: The paradox of targeting
items.blurb: Modern armed forces, using AI-powered decision-support technology like the Maven Smart System, can find targets to strike at an unprecedented pace and scale. It is obviously better to be able to see and strike your enemy before they can do the same to you.

newsletters.title: The NBA Finals we all wanted

items.headline: Victor Wembanyama's emotional reaction to NBA Finals berth
items.blurb: So many athletes try to give off the feeling that they're unaffected by the moment, by the results and by what's in front of them. Maybe it's to be cool? Maybe it's to stay grounded and unbothered in tough situations? Regardless, I greatly appreciate how Victor Wembanyama has decided to let everybody know that outwardly caring is a good thing. It's fun to experience things again.

items.headline: Knicks and Spurs set to duel
items.blurb: Sometimes, the superstar is just too good to be denied, no matter how little experience they may have at the NBA level. That's what happened with Wembanyama and his San Antonio Spurs when they went into Oklahoma City on Saturday to face the Thunder in Game 7. Wembanyama's final Game 7 line wasn't anything too outrageous. He had 22 points (7-of-15 shooting), seven rebounds, two assists and a block in 42 minutes. He never had more than six points in a quarter. And yet, he dominated the night. On the most important possession of the season for the Thunder — down six with less than 40 seconds to go — both Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Cason Wallace bailed out of attacking Wemby in the paint. Stephon Castle's 16 points, six boards and six assists, along with Julian Champagnie's 20 points (six made 3-pointers) and Dylan Harper's 12 points off the bench were enough help to the Spurs complete their season-long torture of the Thunder by the Spurs' hands. Now they head into the NBA Finals for a rematch of the 1999 series against the New York Knicks.

newsletters.title: Bright and colorful fish and lentils

items.headline: Fish and Lentils With Sauce Rof
items.blurb: Instead of cooking lentils and fish separately, she layers them together into a smart one-pot meal laced with the herbal, lemony flavors of Senegalese sauce rof. While the lentils simmer, she marinates the fish in the sauce, letting the fillets absorb the vibrancy of scallions, fresh chiles, garlic and parsley. She adds the fish to the lentils when they're nearly done, so it gently steams without overcooking. Then she finishes everything with a handful of baby spinach wilted on top.

items.headline: Crispy Chicken Thighs With Melty Leeks and Peas
items.blurb: Crackling chicken skin; soft, schmaltz-imbued vegetables; a bright squeeze of lemon. Andy Baraghani's skillet chicken is a crowd-pleasing dinner that's fuss-free and sophisticated.

items.headline: Chile Tofu
items.blurb: From Hetty Lui McKinnon, this is a fiery, forthright and vegan riff on chile paneer, the classic Indo-Chinese stir-fry from Kolkata. Coating the tofu in cornstarch before pan-frying it creates a pronounced crunch, and helps it stand up to the punchy, gingery sauce. Serve it with rice to help tame the flames.

items.headline: Za'atar Chickpea and Tuna Salad
items.blurb: Instead of using a creamy mix of mayo and celery, Ifrah F. Ahmed dresses tuna and chickpeas with olives, za'atar and plenty of fresh dill. It makes a bright, light and speedy lunch or relaxed dinner.

items.headline: Gochujang Buttered Noodles
items.blurb: One of our most popular five-star pantry pastas, this full-flavored dish from Eric Kim can be on the table in under half an hour. Made from a mix of gochujang, honey, garlic and butter, its umami exuberance wins me over every time.

items.headline: German Chocolate Cookies
items.blurb: Almost magically, Samantha Seneviratne shrinks a beloved cake into adorable, fudgy cookies. Dotted with chunks of bittersweet chocolate, pecans and toasted coconut, they're at their best eaten warm from the oven when the chocolate is still a little gooey.

newsletters.title: China has approved the world’s first invasive brain-computer chip—here’s what’s next

items.headline: China has approved the world's first invasive brain-computer chip—here's what's next
items.blurb: Sitting in the courtyard of his house in China's Henan province last October, Dong Hui decided to try holding a pen. Six years after a car accident left him paralyzed from the neck down, he slowly wrote his name, "Thank you," and the date. The breakthrough was made possible by a brain implant called NEO. In March, it became the world's first invasive brain-computer interface approved for use beyond clinical trials. The approval is expected to accelerate China's push to become a global leader in brain implants.

items.headline: Nvidia is launching its first AI chip for personal computers
items.blurb: The RTX Spark will power laptops from Dell, HP, Microsoft, and others. They're being designed specifically to run AI agents. The first devices are set to launch on Windows PCs in the fall. The move marks a challenge to Apple and Intel.

items.headline: The US is stopping exports of AI chips to Chinese firms abroad
items.blurb: It's closed a loophole allowing exports to Chinese subsidiaries, which may have enabled unlicensed access to Nvidia chips. Export curbs have led China to redesign its chip industry.

items.headline: Surgeons have transplanted pig liver and kidneys into a living person
items.blurb: The clinically dead recipient's organs worked for almost five days. Pig organs could ease transplant shortages.

items.headline: The US, Australia, and UK will defend seabed cables with underwater drones
items.blurb: They're developing the vehicles via the trilateral AUKUS defense pact. Undersea internet cables face growing threats.

items.headline: A new study has revealed chatbots' manipulative 'dark patterns'
items.blurb: It found they prey on emotions to encourage harmful behavior. They can also sway voters better than political ads.

items.headline: Texas Tech's survival
items.blurb: The Red Raiders may not be the No. 1 seed in the Women's College World Series — that's Alabama, which we'll talk about in a second — but Texas Tech is clearly the tournament's most interesting team. A group of lovable, rich villains with one of the game's best pitchers anchoring what feels like another charmed run to the title series. The latter point was quite apparent last night, as that pitcher — NiJaree Canady, softball's first seven-figure player — struck out UCLA's Bri Alejandre on a 3-2 pitch with two outs in extra innings to help Tech survive and advance. Next up: a semifinal matchup against top-seeded Bama to win Bracket 1.

items.headline: All of college baseball, really
items.blurb: We've not yet fully reached the super regional weekend of college baseball's postseason, and its No. 1 seed, UCLA, has already been eliminated. No. 2 Georgia Tech has a winner-take-all game today against Oklahoma, which beat the Yellow Jackets 15-8 yesterday. No. 4 Auburn, No. 8 Florida, No. 12 Texas A&M and No. 16 West Virginia face elimination today. No. 9 Southern Miss and No. 13 Nebraska are already toast.

items.headline: Where have these USMNT guys been?
items.blurb: Vibes have been pretty bad for the U.S. team leading up to the start this month of the home World Cup. Friendlies went poorly, the coach is already looking at other jobs and many have long wondered whether this "golden generation" of American soccer talent was really just a mirage. Then Mauricio Pochettino's crew went out and looked sensational — at moments — against Senegal in a World Cup tuneup yesterday, winning 3-2. Christian Pulisic broke his scoring drought and added an assist. It's one match, but you should feel better about the Americans' chances in a couple of weeks after this game.

items.headline: World Cup visa issues arise
items.blurb: The South African national soccer team was supposed to leave Johannesburg yesterday and fly to the United States to prepare for its World Cup-opening match against Mexico on June 11. Instead, the team remained in South Africa to train while officials sort out "grossly unfair" visa issues for some players and personnel. The country's sports minister said they are "being made to look like fools."

items.headline: Yankees score 13 runs in one inning against the Athletics
items.blurb: The Yankees beat the Athletics yesterday 13-8, with all 13 of those runs coming in one inning. It's a first.

breaking_digest.narrative:
A significant shake-up in American media unfolded Sunday when veteran CBS journalist Scott Pelley publicly accused the head of CBS News of "murdering" the venerable newsmagazine "60 Minutes" [1]. The inflammatory charge signals deepening turmoil at the network and raises fresh questions about the future of one of broadcast television's longest-running and most decorated programs. Separately, in the tech and business world, AI startup Anthropic filed to go public, setting the stage for what is expected to be one of the largest IPOs in recent memory and underscoring the continued investor appetite for artificial intelligence companies [2].

On the sports front, Serena Williams announced she will return to professional tennis to compete in a Queen's Club doubles event, marking a notable comeback for the 23-time Grand Slam champion who retired from singles competition in 2022 [3]. Meanwhile, in South America, a far-right outsider candidate advanced in Colombia's presidential election, reflecting a broader regional trend of anti-establishment political momentum and setting up what is expected to be a fiercely contested runoff [4].
